 _Story by Clayton Steward and Justin Perkins_

Adam Hamilton, pastor and founder of Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas
City suburbs, the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States,
walked into a coffee shop in Emporia, Kansas, in late August. With a
population of 24,000, Emporia is roughly the same size as Resurrection's
membership. But instead of preaching, Hamilton was there to make his case for
why he can flip a seat for the U.S. Senate from the Sunflower State, a feat
more than 90 years in the making.

Hamilton told the crowd of about 40 people his campaign is rooted in his faith
and experiences as a pastor but clarified that he is not running to force
people to be Christian or United Methodist. Instead, he is motivated to uphold
the U.S. Constitution and fight for individual rights.

He shared a conversation he had with his wife many times last year.

"Somebody's got to do something," he told her while Trump's cabinet
implemented One Big Beautiful Bill policies and cut funding to groups such as
the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). "After about eight
months of saying somebody's got to do something, she finally turned to me in
January this year and she said, 'Maybe you need to do something.'"

## **Religion and politics collide**

A man in a Navy hat raised his hand at the meet and greet in Emporia. He
explained the day before he had met with his friends of 30 years at the coffee
shop Hamilton's stop was being held at.

"They're Republican, I'm a Democrat. We get along. We have coffee. We go
places together and talk and talk," he said. The man had told his friends
about coming to Hamilton's campaign stop.

"They said, 'He's woke.' I said, 'Well, wasn't Jesus woke?' "

Hamilton's 36-year career as the pastor of a mainline Protestant congregation
puts him in an unusual position as a first-time Democratic candidate. In a
race with sharp political divisions and an enduring rural-urban divide, he is
attempting to bridge a wide coalition of voters based on the ethics of his
theological commitments.

And since he won the ten-person Democratic primary in August, Republicans have
sought to wield Christianity against him. They say he is "too woke" for Kansas
and have even [called him a heretic](https://um-
insight.net/perspectives/hamilton-the-heretic/) for suggesting God would not
condemn people who are not Christians.

This messaging came to a head September 14, when Vice President J.D. Vance
appeared at a campaign rally in Olathe, Kansas, to support Hamilton's
Republican opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall.

Vance accused Hamilton's church of supporting a group of devil worshipers
because of their sponsorship of the Kansas City PrideFest this year. The pride
event included the satirical drag queen performance group Our Ladies of
Perpetual Indulgence, which Vance labeled an "anti-Christian hate group."

The vice president also cherry-picked two 2020 sermons, one in which Hamilton
talked about the Black Lives Matter movement and white privilege, and another
where said Christians need to repent for their destruction of the environment
and acknowledged "maybe changing your diet" as one action.

"Democrat pastor Adam Hamilton thinks it's a sin to be white and a sin to
raise cattle and eat meat, but he's okay with supporting groups that spit on
god-fearing Americans and mock everything that we hold dear," Vance told the
audience. "Ladies and gentlemen, that is not Christianity. That is left-wing
radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion."

In a video response released on September 16, Hamilton said Vance's comments
were part of the "broken politics" that define Washington. As he has done on
the campaign trail, Hamilton presented his D.C. outsider status as the fix.

"These attacks on our faith," he said, "are false and are a sad attempt to
distract from the real hardship facing Kansans." He did not address
Resurrection's support of the KC PrideFest, although the church's website
features a [dedicated page](https://resurrection.church/lgbtq/) for its LGBTQ
ministry, which says, "Resurrection is an LGBTQ friendly church."

Hamilton's response to the vice president instead highlighted Resurrection's
food and health care assistance programs, which the church claims has aided
more than 45,000 people.

"Trying to demean or marginalize the faith of other people, that's just
wrong," he said. "It's also against the Christian teachings to love, serve and
care for one another."

In a 2021 podcast called [Changing My
Position](https://www.theweightpodcast.com/episodes/human-sexuality-changing-
my-position-with-adam-hamilton), Hamilton put his position on sexuality more
clearly. He said that he had spent conservatively "20,000 hours studying the
Bible." As a result, he found, "What is crystal clear is that the driving
ethic of the Christian faith is love, and we're going to love and welcome
people here, gay or straight."

His campaign now depends on whether or not voters resonate with that ethic
extending to the political arena. "I lead from the center," he told the group
gathered in Emporia. "I pastor a church with 9,000 Republicans, 9,000
Democrats and 7,000 independents. I love those Republicans."

## **" Doc" Marshall**

In a debate before hundreds at the Kansas state fair September 12, Hamilton's
incumbent Republican opponent Roger Marshall launched a similar line of
attack.

Born in El Dorado, Kansas, Marshall practiced medicine as an obstetrician-
gynecologist in Great Bend, Kansas, in Barton County, for more than 25 years.
Marshall was first elected to Congress in 2016 to serve Kansas' rural 1st
Congressional District until he was elected to the Senate in 2021. Endorsed by
Trump, Marshall contrasts his rural bona fides against Hamilton's suburban
background.

"My opponent is too woke, he's too weak and he doesn't stand for anything,"
Marshall said. He blamed the Democratic party for having "strangled the ag
industry," saying that if Hamilton had his way, "he'd go put a plastic bag
over the mouths of these dairy cows back here," motioning to the livestock
building on the fairgrounds.

Despite his spar with Hamilton, Marshall spent much of the debate struggling
against the crowd. Videos recorded of the debate showed Marshall's answers
overwhelmed by jeers and boos from the crowd.

Days earlier, the New York Times reported that Marshall and his OBGYN practice
had sued more than 700 patients over their inability to pay for care. Eighty-
one of those cases resulted in arrests, including a couple who were arrested
on Easter weekend for being unable to pay a $4,561 bill for an emergency
hysterectomy.

The Times found Marshall routinely charged patients an 18% annual interest
rate on unpaid bills ranging from $101 to several thousand dollars. Patients
also had their paychecks and bank accounts garnished. Most of the patients
sued lived in rural Barton County, including many who lacked insurance.

At the state fair, Marshall attempted to defend his billing record, saying
"those were common, common business practices. We would go a year before we
would ever send somebody over." But the crowd was not buying it and erupted in
chants of "shame on you!"

## **A vital seat for Democrats**

Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George
McGill was elected during the Great Depression. But voters have elected some
high-profile Democrats in recent years, including two-term Gov. Laura Kelly
and four-term U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids.

Hamilton believes he can join them by pushing a platform of broad appeal:
lowering costs, strengthening consumer protection laws, stopping D.C.
corruption and combating the tariffs and health care cuts championed by
President Donald Trump in the One Big Beautiful Bill.

If Democrats hold all their current senate seats and can flip four held by
Republicans, they can retake the Senate in November.

While Marshall remains the favorite, recent polls show an unexpectedly tight
race for Republicans. A [September poll by Emerson College Polling/Nexstar
Media](https://emersoncollegepolling.com/kansas-2026/) gives Hamilton a two-
point lead over Marshall. It is the first independent survey of the cycle to
show Hamilton leading.

"This poll finds Democrats with their best chance to win their first Senate
seat in Kansas since 1932, in part driven by Democrat Hamilton's appeal to
independent voters, leading by 15 points," said Spencer Kimball, executive
director of Emerson College Polling, in a statement accompanying the survey.
The poll of likely voters also found 8% are undecided, with 4% supporting
Libertarian David Graham. About half of respondents identified the economy as
their top issue.

In August, Cook Political Report shifted the Kansas race in Hamilton's favor
from "solid Republican" to "lean Republican."

A July poll by GBAO Strategies in Washington D.C. found Marshall's close
affiliation with President Trump hurt his favorability. Over half of the
polled individuals said they do not want a "yes man" for Trump elected as
their next senator.

In a sign of shifting party divisions, former Kansas GOP Governor Bill Graves
[endorsed Hamilton](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/former-kansas-gop-
governor-explains-why-hes-backing-democrat-adam-hamilton-for-senate) in late
September, saying Marshall simply amounted to a "yes-vote" for the Trump
administration. At the same time, Hamilton urged former Vice President Kamala
Harris to stay out of his campaign, saying in an interview with MS NOW, "We
are a different kind of Democrat."

Flipping a key seat requires not only campaign stops, endorsements and good
polling numbers, but also money. Hamilton told the Emporia coffee shop crowd
it will take $20 million to run a successful campaign. The crowd let out
cheers when he asked if they had heard of a guy named Talarico.

"You're a cheap date in Kansas," a New York donor told Hamilton when comparing
his $20 million goal to Talarico's $160 million goal.

Hamilton has raised just over $4 million, largely from individuals, according
to FEC filings. Marshall has raised more than $6 million including $2.7
million in support from PACs ranging from the Mississippi Farm Bureau and the
health care industry to the Teamsters Union PAC.

## **Who will represent rural Kansas?**

"I was raised in Johnson County," Hamilton told the crowd in Emporia. "I'm
really sorry about that," poking fun at his childhood in suburban Kansas City.
It's a much different Kansas experience than much of Kansas where rolling
hills are dotted with pump jacks, cattle, late summer wildflowers, and wind
turbines this time of year.

Hamilton feels like he is gaining the pulse of rural Kansas after an estimated
40 campaign stops across the state before Emporia.

"Our ag industry is the number one industry in the state," he said in an
interview with Barn Raiser. "If you as a senator are not caring about ag and
the ag industry and the people in rural America, you're not doing your job."

For his part, Marshall spent most of August traveling across 59 Kansas
counties speaking with farmers, ranchers, doctors, manufacturers, small
business owners and families as part of his "120 Stops to Strengthen Rural
Kansas" tour.

He is concerned about the high costs for fuel and fertilizer as well as the
impacts tariffs have on farmers and ranchers. The decision to lift tariffs and
import foreign beef had not been announced at the time of that interview.

Hamilton is also concerned about the state of rural hospitals. Kansas leads
the nation in rural hospitals that are at risk of immediate closure due to the
passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill last year. Marshall championed his vote
for the bill at the time, which made nearly $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid
through 2035. In 2025, United Methodist Health Ministry Fund estimated that
Kansas stood to lose nearly $4 billion in federal and state Medicaid funding.

The bill also provided a one-time $50 billion distributed over five years in
the Rural Health Transformation Program. Kansas received $221 million for the
program's first year, far short of the funds needed to offset the Medicaid
cuts.

In 2024, over 240,000 Kansans were uninsured, a statistically higher rate than
the rest of the country.

In a statement released after his rural Kansas tour, Marshall said, "We've got
a lot to be proud of--from cutting taxes for working families and growing
Kansas manufacturing to delivering real resources for our rural hospitals.

Will a politics of human decency outweigh party loyalty among voters?

Hamilton believes so. At a campaign stop in Greensburg, he recalled one woman
who told him, "I want somebody who's going to help me not hate my neighbors
anymore," he told the crowd in Emporia.

Short-haired, elderly women held down the front row of chairs while Hamilton
spoke. They occasionally responded to a question posed by Hamilton, regularly
giving a classic Midwestern shake of the head in support or disgust.

Among those in the front row was former English teacher, Sharol Cutrell. After
Hamilton spoke, she told him she didn't vote for him in the primaries.

"I would vote for him today," she told Barn Raiser. "Everything I believe,
he's right in line with. And we need somebody like that, somebody neutral,
who's for people who don't have as much as we do."

Cutrell had concerns about voting for a megachurch pastor in the primary, a
sentiment shared by others in the coffee shop that morning. Seeing him in
person made her believe he is the right nominee for the challenge.

When introducing themselves to Hamilton, many folks gave a brief outline of
their family tree, starting with their abolitionist and settler roots in
Kansas. A sunflower was incorporated into the design of the banner on the Lyon
County Democrats office across the street.

In November voters will choose between two fifth-generation Kansans: a MAGA-
backed Republican doctor and a Democrat mainline Protestant pastor.

"Keep me in your prayers," Hamilton said to a woman as he left the event.
